summary: 18 claims on heat stress at work, each checked against a fetched page or PDF. They cover ILO 2019 and 2024, Lancet Countdown 2025, WBGT dose-response, injury uplift on hot days, the Saudi midday ban and its effects, NIOSH and CDC guidance, and OSHA and Cal/OSHA cost-benefit numbers. Two links matter most for the story. Most heat harm happens outside heatwaves, and the fixed Saudi ban window (12:00 to 15:00) misses the 9 am to 12 pm WBGT peak found on Saudi sites, so real-time WBGT monitoring adds value. No Saudi-specific injury, death or Lancet value was found.

claims.topic: ILO 2019: working hours, jobs and money lost to heat in 2030
claims.figure: 2.2% of total working hours lost in 2030 (80 million full-time jobs, US$2,400 billion); agriculture 60% and construction 19% of that loss
claims.measures: Status: stat (projection). Share of global working hours lost to heat stress at 1.5 C of warming, with agriculture and construction work assumed to be in the shade. The full report (printed p.13, PDF at https://www.ilo.org/sites/default/files/wcmsp5/groups/public/@dgreports/@dcomm/@publ/documents/publication/wcms_711919.pdf) also gives US$280 billion for 1995 and, if that work is done in the sun, 3.8% of hours and 136 million jobs. Sector shares are on printed p.14.
claims.source_title: Increase in heat stress predicted to bring productivity loss equivalent to 80 million jobs (news release for 'Working on a warmer planet')
claims.quote: 2.2 per cent of total working hours worldwide will be lost because of higher temperatures, a loss equivalent to 80 million full-time jobs
claims.use_in_story: Run a counter up to 2.2% of hours, then 80 million jobs, then a US$2,400 billion bar, and split the loss into a 60% farm slice and a 19% construction slice.

claims.topic: ILO 2019: Saudi Arabia and Arab States working hours lost to heat
claims.figure: Saudi Arabia: 0.5% of working hours lost in 2030 (69.3 thousand full-time jobs), up from 0.2% in 1995. Arab States: 1.0% (618.0 thousand jobs)
claims.measures: Status: stat (projection). Table 5.1, printed p.51 (PDF page 49 of 98). Row columns are 1995 then 2030: agriculture, industry, construction, services, total %, total thousand full-time jobs. Saudi 2030 construction is 1.6% and services 0.2%. Other 2030 totals: Qatar 5.3%, Bahrain 4.1%, UAE 2.6%, Kuwait 1.0%, Oman 0.5%. Agriculture and construction work is assumed to be in the shade. Construction is expected to be 40% of hours lost in the Arab States in 2030. Arab States GDP loss: 0.5% in 1995 and 1.1% in 2030.
claims.source_title: Working on a warmer planet: The impact of heat stress on labour productivity and decent work (Table 5.1)
claims.use_in_story: Show a Gulf bar chart of 2030 hours lost, with Saudi Arabia at 0.5% beside Qatar at 5.3%, and note that construction drives 40% of the Arab States loss.

claims.topic: ILO 2024: workers, injuries and deaths from excessive heat
claims.figure: 2.41 billion workers exposed a year; 22.85 million injuries and 18,970 deaths a year attributable to excessive heat
claims.measures: Status: stat. Global estimates, 2020 data. Also 2.09 million DALYs (disability-adjusted life years) a year (PDF page 6 of the report at a glance). The ILO news release of 22 Apr 2024 (https://www.ilo.org/resource/news/climate-change-creates-%E2%80%98cocktail%E2%80%99-serious-health-hazards-70-cent-world%E2%80%99s) adds 70.9% of the global workforce exposed, up from 65.5% in 2000, and 26.2 million people living with chronic kidney disease linked to workplace heat stress (2020 figures). That release prints 22.87 million injuries. The report summary and later ILO and WHO pages print 22.85 million.
claims.source_title: Ensuring safety and health at work in a changing climate: Report at a glance
claims.quote: Every year, 22.85 million occupational injuries, 18,970 work-related deaths, and 2.09 million DALYs attributable to excessive heat.
claims.use_in_story: Show 2.41 billion worker dots and end on a counter of 18,970 lives lost each year.

claims.topic: ILO 2024: share of Arab States workers exposed to excessive heat
claims.figure: 83.6% of the Arab States workforce exposed to excessive heat, against a global average of 71%
claims.measures: Status: stat. 2020 data from the ILO report 'Heat at work: Implications for safety and health', described in an ILO news item of 25 Jul 2024. Same page: Africa 92.9% and Asia and the Pacific 74.7%.
claims.source_title: More workers than ever are losing the fight against heat stress
claims.quote: Workplace exposures to excessive heat in the Arab States were above the global average, affecting 83.6 per cent of the workforce.
claims.use_in_story: Fill a regional gauge to 83.6% for the Arab States, with a tick at the 71% global average.

claims.topic: ILO 2024: most heat injuries happen outside heatwaves
claims.figure: 8 in 10 occupational injuries from extreme heat happen outside heatwaves; 9 in 10 workers are exposed to excessive heat outside a heatwave
claims.measures: Status: stat. Same ILO page and report as the Arab States figure (2020 data). The page also says 4,200 workers died from heatwaves in 2020. That is a different estimate from the 18,970 deaths from all excessive heat, so do not add the two.
claims.source_title: More workers than ever are losing the fight against heat stress
claims.quote: eight in ten occupational injuries from extreme heat happened outside of heatwaves
claims.use_in_story: Animate a calendar where only a few days are heatwave days, then land most injury markers on the ordinary hot days, to argue for monitoring every shift.

claims.topic: Lancet Countdown 2025: work hours and income lost to heat in 2024
claims.figure: 639 billion potential work hours lost to heat in 2024 (98% above 1990-99); US$1.09 trillion potential income loss (0.99% of global GDP)
claims.measures: Status: stat (modelled potential loss). Global, 2024, indicators 1.1.3 and 4.1.3 (accepted manuscript, PDF pages 8, 26, 27, 73 and 74). Same report: construction is 17.7% of potential hours lost and 28% of income losses; agriculture is 63.5% and 39%. The Lancet press release of 28 Oct 2025 (https://www.eurekalert.org/news-releases/1103130) prints the same headline. The report gives no Saudi or Middle East value.
claims.source_title: The 2025 report of the Lancet Countdown on health and climate change: climate change action offers a lifeline (accepted manuscript)
claims.publisher: The Lancet Countdown (manuscript hosted by LSE Research Online)
claims.quote: 639 billion potential work hours were lost to heat exposure alone in 2024, 98% above the 1990–99 average, costing US$ 1.09 trillion
claims.use_in_story: Tick a clock face up to 639 billion hours, stack a US$1.09 trillion bar beside it, then zoom into the 28% construction slice.

claims.topic: Kjellstrom et al. 2009: work capacity versus WBGT
claims.figure: Heavy work (class 3, about 400 W): 27 C WBGT needs no rest; 29.5 C needs 50% rest (50% work capacity); 31.5 C needs 75% rest (25% capacity); 36 C means no work
claims.measures: Status: stat. Table 2 of the paper, for acclimatised workers in light clothing. Work capacity is the share of each hour a worker can work. Medium work (class 2, about 300 W): 28 C continuous, 30.5 C for 50% rest, 32 C for 75% rest, 37 C no work. Light work (about 200 W): 31, 32, 32.5 and 39 C for the same steps. The abstract says capacity falls quickly once WBGT passes 26 to 30 C. Values come from the ISO heat stress standard and NIOSH recommendations. Cross-check with a different curve: ILO 2019 (printed p.13) says a worker at moderate intensity loses 50% of capacity at 33 to 34 C. DOI 10.3402/gha.v2i0.2047, PMC2799237.
claims.source_title: Workplace heat stress, health and productivity: an increasing challenge for low and middle-income countries during climate change (Global Health Action 2009;2:2047)
claims.publisher: Global Health Action (Taylor & Francis), full text via Europe PMC
claims.quote: Recommended maximum WBGT exposure levels (°C) at different work intensities and rest/work ratios for an average acclimatised worker wearing light clothing
claims.use_in_story: Draw a thermometer climbing from 27 to 31.5 C WBGT while a worker bar shrinks from 100% to 25% capacity.

claims.topic: WHO and WMO 2025: productivity lost per degree of heat
claims.figure: Worker productivity drops by 2-3% for every degree C above 20 C
claims.measures: Status: stat. Statement in the WHO and WMO news release of 22 Aug 2025 on 'Climate change and workplace heat stress: technical report and guidance'. The sentence does not name the heat index, so check the full report before pairing it with WBGT. Cross-check: a 2018 meta-analysis of 111 studies (Lancet Planetary Health, DOI 10.1016/s2542-5196(18)30237-7, abstract via https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/search?query=EXT_ID:30526938%20AND%20SRC:MED&resultType=core&format=json) found that 30% of workers under heat stress reported productivity losses and that heat strain was 4.01 times more likely.
claims.source_title: WHO, WMO issue new report and guidance to protect workers from increasing heat stress
claims.publisher: World Health Organization (WHO) and World Meteorological Organization (WMO)
claims.quote: Worker productivity drops by 2–3% for every degree above 20°C.
claims.use_in_story: Draw a sloped line from 20 C upward and drop an output bar by 2 to 3 points at each degree.

claims.topic: Park, Pankratz and Behrer 2021: injury risk on hot days
claims.figure: Injury risk rises 5-7% on 85-90 F days and 10-15% above 100 F, against days in the 60s F. About 20,000 extra injuries a year in California
claims.measures: Status: stat. California workers' compensation claims, 2001-2018 (IZA Discussion Paper 14560, July 2021). The percentages are on printed p.2. The 360,000 extra injuries over 2001-2018, roughly 20,000 a year, are on printed p.3. Effects show up indoors and outdoors and for injuries not usually blamed on heat. Cross-check: a 2025 US national study of 2023 OSHA injury cases (Environmental Health, DOI 10.1186/s12940-025-01231-1, abstract via https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/search?query=PMCID:PMC12498468&resultType=core&format=json) found odds ratios of 1.03 at heat index 90 F or more, 1.10 at 100 F or more and 1.20 at 110 F or more, against 80 F.
claims.source_title: Temperature, Workplace Safety, and Labor Market Inequality (IZA Discussion Paper No. 14560)
claims.quote: A day with high temperatures between 85 and 90 F leads to a 5 to 7 percent increase in same-day injury risk
claims.use_in_story: Animate a risk curve that bends up at 85 F and steepens past 100 F, with injury markers appearing on hot days.

claims.topic: Saudi midday outdoor work ban: dates, hours and 2025 compliance
claims.figure: Ban on outdoor work under the sun from 15 June to 15 September 2026, 12:00 to 15:00, for all private-sector establishments; 94% compliance in 2025
claims.measures: Status: stat (regulation in force). Set by the Ministry of Human Resources and Social Development with the National Council for Occupational Safety and Health. Violations can be reported on 19911. Employers must provide drinking water, rest areas, shade and protective equipment. The 2024 season had 94.6% compliance under Ministerial Decision No. 3337 of 15/7/1435 AH (https://www.hrsd.gov.sa/en/media-center/news/150920244). ILO 2019 (printed p.52) says all GCC countries have adopted a midday work ban.
claims.source_title: Implementation of the Midday Work Ban Decision Begins on 15 June
claims.publisher: Ministry of Human Resources and Social Development (HRSD), Saudi Arabia
claims.quote: effective from Monday, 15 June 2026, until Tuesday, 15 September 2026, from 12:00 p.m. to 3:00 p.m.
claims.use_in_story: Shade a 12:00 to 15:00 block on a day-long timeline and stamp 15 June to 15 September on a Saudi calendar.

claims.topic: Saudi midday work ban: 2026 season results
claims.figure: 29,945 inspection visits, 95% compliance, 1,771 violations and 41 reports handled in the 2026 season
claims.measures: Status: stat. Ministry figures as reported by Arab News on 15 Sep 2026. CairoScene (17 Sep 2026, https://cairoscene.com/News/2026-Summer-Midday-Work-Ban-Lifted-for-Private-Sector-in-Saudi-Arabia) prints the same numbers. The ministry's own end-of-season release for 2026 was not found.
claims.source_title: Saudi Arabia ends 2026 midday work ban
claims.quote: the ministry conducted 29,945 inspection visits across the Kingdom, with establishments recording a 95 percent compliance rate
claims.use_in_story: Run the season as a progress bar to 15 September, then reveal 29,945 visits, 95% compliance and 1,771 violations.

claims.topic: Saudi construction sites: the ban window misses the hottest hours
claims.figure: Hourly mean WBGT of 31-33 C peaked from 9 am to 12 pm, before the 12-3 pm ban; complying with the ban did not reduce heat stress risk
claims.measures: Status: stat. Field study at 10 residential construction sites in Al-Ahsa Province, June to September 2016, scored against ACGIH guidelines (Annals of Work Exposures and Health 2019, DOI 10.1093/annweh/wxz033). A small study in one province. ILO 2019 (printed p.52) also warns that temperatures stay extremely high outside the banned hours and that limited inspection weakens the ban. It suggests a ban tied to real-time temperature, humidity and workload.
claims.source_title: Assessment of Heat Stress Exposure among Construction Workers in the Hot Desert Climate of Saudi Arabia
claims.publisher: Annals of Work Exposures and Health (abstract via Europe PMC)
claims.quote: Complying with a midday outdoor work ban (12-3 p.m.) was not effective in reducing heat stress risk.
claims.use_in_story: Overlay a WBGT curve on the 12-3 pm ban block and highlight the 9 am to 12 pm peak that the ban does not cover.

claims.topic: Saudi construction workers: kidney injury over one summer
claims.figure: 18% incidence of kidney injury among 65 construction workers between June and September 2016
claims.measures: Status: stat. Al-Ahsa Province. Kidney injury was defined as a urinary albumin-creatinine ratio of 30 mg/g or more. Risk factors were dehydration, short sleep and obesity (International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health 2020, DOI 10.3390/ijerph17113775). Small cohort. ILO 2019 (printed p.52) cites a survey of Nepalese migrant workers in Qatar, the UAE and Saudi Arabia in which 17.6% said they suffered from heat-related illness.
claims.source_title: Risk of Kidney Injury among Construction Workers Exposed to Heat Stress: A Longitudinal Study from Saudi Arabia
claims.publisher: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health (abstract via Europe PMC)
claims.quote: A significant increase in ACR occurred among most workers over the study period; incidence of KI was 18%.
claims.use_in_story: Show 65 worker icons and light up the 18% who developed kidney injury as the bar moves from June to September.

claims.topic: NIOSH 2016: WBGT limits and work/rest ratios
claims.figure: Moderate work: NIOSH REL is 27.8 C WBGT (82 F) for acclimatised workers and 25 C (77 F) for unacclimatised workers. At WBGT 90 F or more, moderate work (425 W) is 20 minutes of work and 40 minutes of rest each hour
claims.measures: Status: stat (guidance). NIOSH Criteria for a Recommended Standard, DHHS (NIOSH) Publication 2016-106. Worked example on printed p.4. Formulas on p.93, with M as metabolic rate in watts: RAL = 59.9 - 14.1 log10 M and REL = 56.7 - 11.5 log10 M. Work/rest and water table on p.104 (Table 8-1, adapted from a US Defense Department table). OSHA's proposed rule would use heat index 80 F or WBGT at the NIOSH RAL as the initial heat trigger, and heat index 90 F or WBGT at the REL as the high heat trigger (https://www.osha.gov/sites/default/files/Heat-Rulemaking-NPRM-Presentation.pdf). ACGIH numeric tables are copyrighted and were not found in public sources.
claims.source_title: Criteria for a Recommended Standard: Occupational Exposure to Heat and Hot Environments (Revised Criteria 2016)
claims.publisher: US National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health (NIOSH), CDC
claims.quote: a vertical line at 300 kcal·h-1 (348.9 W) intersects the 60 min·h-1 REL curve at a WBGT of 27.8°C (82°F)
claims.use_in_story: Draw two alert lines on a WBGT dial, 25 C for new workers and 27.8 C for acclimatised workers, and flip the work/rest split as the needle climbs.

claims.topic: CDC and NIOSH: hydration and acclimatisation
claims.figure: 1 cup (8 oz) of water every 15-20 minutes; no more than 6 cups per hour; new workers start at 20% of the usual heat exposure on day 1
claims.measures: Status: stat (guidance). CDC/NIOSH Workplace Recommendations page, last updated 16 Jul 2026. The cup rule is for moderate activity in heat lasting under 2 hours. Experienced workers: 50%, 60%, 80% and 100% of the usual duration on days 1 to 4. New workers add no more than 20% a day. The 2016 NIOSH criteria (https://www.cdc.gov/niosh/docs/2016-106/pdfs/2016-106.pdf, printed p.82 and p.104) give the same cup rule and cap fluid at 1.5 quarts an hour and 12 quarts a day.
claims.publisher: US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC/NIOSH)
claims.quote: drink 1 cup (8 oz.) of water every 15–20 minutes
claims.use_in_story: Pulse a water-cup icon every 15 to 20 minutes along a shift timeline.

claims.topic: OSHA 2024 proposed heat rule: cost, deaths and injuries prevented
claims.figure: US$7.8 billion a year in cost; 531 heat deaths and 16,027 heat injuries or illnesses prevented a year; US$9.179 billion a year in benefits
claims.measures: Status: stat (projection in a proposed rule, not final). 89 Federal Register 70698, 30 Aug 2024. Cost is on p.70824 (2023 dollars, 2% discount rate) and about 36 million workers are covered (p.70740). Benefits are on pp.70802-70803 and 70967: US$7.310 billion from deaths valued at US$13.77 million each and US$1.869 billion from injuries valued at US$116,588 each. OSHA estimates 559 deaths and 24,656 illnesses a year after correcting for undercounting (factors 14 and 7.5), against about 40 deaths and 3,288 illnesses recorded. OSHA's rulemaking page (https://www.osha.gov/heat-exposure/rulemaking) lists the hearing as ended 2 Jul 2025 and post-hearing comments as closed 30 Oct 2025.
claims.source_title: Heat Injury and Illness Prevention in Outdoor and Indoor Work Settings (proposed rule, Federal Register Vol. 89, No. 169)
claims.publisher: US Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA), Department of Labor
claims.quote: would prevent 531 heat-related fatalities (of the estimated 559 annual fatalities) and 16,027 HRIs per year
claims.use_in_story: Balance a US$7.8 billion cost block against a US$9.179 billion benefit block, with 531 lives and 16,027 injuries ticking up beside it.

claims.topic: Cal/OSHA indoor heat standard: cost versus benefit
claims.figure: Benefits of US$404 million a year (US$4.0 billion over 10 years), 57% of it productivity gains, against direct costs of about US$1.0 billion over 10 years
claims.measures: Status: stat (projection for a proposed rule). Initial Statement of Reasons for California's indoor heat standard, hearing 18 May 2023, pages 24 to 26 of 30. Cost sentence: 'approximately $1.0 billion over 10 years (with a range of $0.7 to $1.3 billion)'. Benefits range from US$2.6 to 6.8 billion over 10 years, undiscounted: US$2.3 billion productivity and US$1.7 billion health. The figures are for the proposal text and were not checked against the adopted rule.
claims.source_title: Heat Illness Prevention in Indoor Places of Employment: Initial Statement of Reasons
claims.publisher: California Occupational Safety and Health Standards Board (Cal/OSHA)
claims.quote: The primary estimate of the total direct benefits is $404 million (with a range from $257 to $678 million) on an undiscounted annualized basis
claims.use_in_story: Show productivity as the largest slice of the payback bar to argue that heat control pays for itself, not only saves lives.

claims.topic: Construction share of US heat deaths
claims.figure: Construction is 7% of the US workforce but accounts for over one-third of occupational heat deaths (34.0%, 18 deaths in 2023)
claims.measures: Status: stat. CPWR Data Bulletin, August 2025, using BLS fatal injury data. Construction's fatal heat injury rate was nearly four times that of other industries (0.15 versus 0.04 per 100,000 full-time workers). Heat deaths of all US workers rose 77.4% from 2012 to 2023 (31 to 55). OSHA slides (https://www.osha.gov/sites/default/files/Heat-Rulemaking-NPRM-Presentation.pdf) cite 479 recorded US heat deaths in 2011-2022, about 40 a year.
claims.source_title: Data Bulletin: Heat Injuries and Illnesses among Construction Workers
claims.publisher: CPWR, The Center for Construction Research and Training
claims.quote: Although construction workers are only 7% of the overall workforce, they account for more than one-third of occupational heat-related deaths.
claims.use_in_story: Show 7 of every 100 workers in hard hats, then show about one in three heat-death markers wearing hard hats.

gaps: No Saudi or Middle East value for potential labour hours or income lost to heat in the Lancet Countdown 2025 global report text. Country data sits on the Lancet Countdown data explorer (https://lancetcountdown.org/explore-our-data/), which was not fetched.

No Saudi heat-specific injury or death count was found. GASTAT 'Health and Safety at Workplace Statistics 2024' gives only all-cause rates of 245.7 non-fatal and 1.1 fatal occupational injuries per 100 thousand workers (https://stats.gov.sa/documents/20117/2435273/Health+and+Safety+at+Workplace+Statistics+2024+EN+(1).pdf/96c86c8f-6b92-ed61-f76f-dcc583d08c2a?t=1756901388615). Heat is not itemised.
No GCC ministry count of heat-illness cases was found. Gulf evidence is limited to two small Saudi studies (65 workers; 10 sites) and an ILO-cited survey (17.6%).
ACGIH TLV and Action Limit numeric tables are copyrighted. The OSHA Technical Manual says they are not public. NIOSH REL, RAL and ISO-based values are used instead.
The ministry's own 2026 end-of-season release for the Saudi midday ban was not found. The 2026 results rely on Arab News and CairoScene.

The 2-3% per degree above 20 C is quoted from the WHO and WMO news release. The WHO full technical report (WHO IRIS) returned HTTP 403, so the index behind the 20 C (air temperature or WBGT) is unconfirmed. The 2018 meta-analysis full text was not reachable; only its abstract was read.

The ILO 2024 full report (46 MB) was not fetched. The 26.2 million kidney disease figure and the 70.9% share come from the ILO news release. The release prints 22.87 million injuries while the report summary prints 22.85 million.

The Lancet journal site returned HTTP 403. Lancet figures come from the LSE-hosted accepted manuscript and the Lancet press release on EurekAlert. Some secondary summaries print different HDI-group GDP shares than the manuscript, so those were not used.

OSHA's own PEA PDF is over 10 MB and could not be fetched. The Federal Register PDF on govinfo carries the same text. The Federal Register website redirected to an unblock page and was not followed. OSHA's rule status after Oct 2025 is from trackers only: a supplemental proposal is said to be targeted for Dec 2026, not verified at DOL.
Cal/OSHA figures are from the 2023 proposal text. The Department of Finance summary PDF was an empty form, so the adopted rule's cost-benefit figures were not checked.
Injury-versus-heat dose-response data are from California and the US as a whole. No Gulf or Saudi dose-response study was found. The ILO Arab States estimates use global exposure-response curves.
PubMed and PMC pages showed robot checks and some publisher pages returned HTTP 403. Abstracts and full text were read through the Europe PMC API instead.
